headline: New Hampshire doctors report an early start to flu season
dek: Clinicians around the state are seeing influenza cases earlier than usual, while national surveillance shows activity rising but still low and health officials urge vaccination before circulation builds.
body: Influenza is showing up in New Hampshire medical centers earlier than doctors typically expect, giving residents a reason to think about vaccination before the usual late-October and November buildup. New Hampshire Public Radio reported Friday that clinicians have seen cases beginning in September, particularly influenza A, rather than waiting for the more familiar fall-to-winter increase.

The local picture is still preliminary. NHPR reported that several medical centers had seen about two dozen cases in all, based on accounts from the facilities, and Southern New Hampshire Medical Center said it had recorded 19 cases across its care centers. Dr. Gabriela Andujar Vazquez, Dartmouth Health’s medical director for infection prevention and control, told NHPR that the health system had not seen flu cases in September last year but has had patients with flu earlier this year. She described the activity as still low while trending upward.

That distinction matters because an early signal is not the same as a statewide outbreak. The [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Week 39 report](https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/2026-week-39.html), covering the week that ended Oct. 3, said seasonal influenza activity remained low nationally even as several surveillance measures increased. The CDC reported that 3.6% of specimens tested by clinical laboratories were positive for flu, up from the previous week, and said activity was increasing across multiple indicators from late August and early September. The agency also cautioned that all of the surveillance data are preliminary.

The national report points to influenza A as the dominant virus in the early data. Of 204 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories during Week 39, 201 were influenza A and three were influenza B. Among the influenza A viruses that were subtyped, 125 of 127 were identified as A(H1N1)pdm09. Those figures describe tested specimens and circulating viruses; they do not provide a New Hampshire case count and should not be read as a forecast of how severe the state’s season will become.

For New Hampshire families, the practical issue is timing. The CDC recommends seasonal flu vaccination for people six months and older and says vaccination should ideally be offered before the end of October. The protection is not immediate: clinicians told NHPR that it takes roughly two weeks for immunity to build. Dr. Susan Hills, operational director for Southern New Hampshire Medical Center’s immediate-care locations, said the vaccine’s main benefit is reducing the severity of illness, rather than guaranteeing that a vaccinated person cannot become infected.

Doctors are paying particular attention to people more likely to develop complications, including adults 65 and older, pregnant people and those with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart disease. Hills told NHPR that people in those groups who develop symptoms should seek testing promptly because antiviral treatment is most useful when started early. The report also described flu as an illness that can arrive suddenly, with body aches and fever, although symptoms vary.

The timing of this season remains uncertain. CDC data show the highest activity in the West and low overall levels nationally, while New Hampshire clinicians are reporting an earlier start in their own facilities. More weeks of testing and state-level surveillance will be needed to show whether those early cases grow into sustained community spread. In the meantime, staying home when sick, washing hands and wearing a mask can reduce transmission, and residents can check with a clinician or pharmacy about vaccination options.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire doctors report early flu season activity
seoDescription: New Hampshire clinicians report early flu cases as CDC surveillance shows activity rising but still low and vaccination guidance points to late October.
